job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Elena Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Elena, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior developer at a 14-person startup in Marenco, the port city. We build booking software for small freight forwarders. I graduated in software engineering in June and did a three-month internship at a bank's app team before that. A normal day is a stand-up at 9:30, then I fix bugs or build a small screen with my AI coding assistant open beside me, then I review code with our lead, Anselm. I rent a room in a flat with two strangers who became friends. The loan and the rent eat most of my salary, and I try not to look at my bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, just not the revolution everyone shouted about. I already use a coding assistant every day, so I'd say it saves me maybe an hour and sometimes costs me an hour fixing its mistakes. Online I'd probably post a funny screenshot of a wrong answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, plateau is the comfortable version, but comfortable isn't safe. Our startup has eight months of money left, and a funding round that isn't signed. If the round falls through, I'm out, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep shipping features and keep learning the backend side, because juniors who can do only the front end are easy to replace. I'd build a small side project, maybe a tool for small shipping agents, on weekends. And I'd keep three months of rent aside, which I don't have yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit jittery, mostly about the funding round, but I'm not panicking. I like my job, so I feel lucky and nervous together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly worries you about the funding round, and what's your fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anselm told us the round closes in January. If it doesn't, we get one month's notice. That's about 2,200 pounds that I'd need to stretch, and I'd look for a contract role right away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the side project serious or a hobby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my flatmate Sora, who works in a hospital's IT team, if they're hiring. And I'd update my profile today rather than on the day it's needed. It's not a plan so much as a habit.

say: I'd say AI is **useful** but not a revolution, and post a funny screenshot of its mistakes.
At work I'd mention it saves me an hour and sometimes **costs** one.
think: Plateau is comfortable but not **safe**, because our startup's money runs out in eight months.
If the funding round fails, I'm out, whatever **AI** does.
do: Learn the **backend** side so I'm not just a front-end junior.
Build a small tool for shipping agents as a **side project** on weekends.
Set aside **three months** of rent, which I don't have yet.
feel: I feel **jittery** about the funding round, lucky and nervous together.
S0.quote: Our startup has eight months of money left, and a funding round that isn't signed.
fieldNote: Elena's threat is **startup funding**, not AI, and she keeps a fallback habit of updating her profile early.
She is a daily AI user and talks about it with mild humour.
The side project shows a pattern: she hedges by building.

steps.text: Learn backend development alongside the front-end work
Build a small booking tool for shipping agents on weekends
Set aside three months of rent in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and I'm living in it. At work I'd tell Anselm we should rewrite how we hire, because a junior with an assistant now does what two did. Online I'd say governments need to fund retraining before the cuts, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm a junior developer, which is exactly the kind of job being squeezed. I'm good with the tools, so I might be fine, but I can see the companies thinking they need fewer juniors. The seniors will stay, the interns will go, and I'm in the middle with a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to become the person on the team who knows how to check what the AI writes, because that's the skill I think will stay. I'd take a cloud security course online for 200 pounds, and I'd put my side project on a public page to show what I can build alone. And I'd join the developers' union group, since I want a say in how our firm uses these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and scared in about equal parts. It's like being on a fast train that you can steer a little. I like that I can adapt, but I know adapting doesn't pay my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about someone you know who's already been affected.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Marguerite from uni couldn't find a job for five months. She's smart, but every posting wanted three years of experience. That's what frightens me about the new world: nobody wants to train juniors, because the assistant does the easy work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change if you could make one rule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I could make one rule, it would be that firms must take on a number of entry-level people for every certain number of staff. I'd vote for whoever proposes that.

say: I'd say it's real and I'm **living in it**, and firms should rethink how they hire.
Online I'd say governments must fund **retraining** before the cuts.
think: Juniors are exactly the kind of job being **squeezed**, even if I'm good with the tools.
Seniors stay, interns go, and I'm in the **middle** with a loan.
do: Become the person who **checks** what the AI writes.
Take a **cloud security** course online for 200 pounds.
Put my side project on a **public page** and join the developers' union group.
feel: I feel **excited** and scared in equal parts, like steering a fast train a little.
S1.quote: Nobody wants to train juniors, because the assistant does the easy work.
fieldNote: Elena sees her own exposure clearly and answers with **adaptation plus collective voice**.
Her friend Marguerite's five-month search makes the entry-level squeeze personal.
She backs a rule forcing firms to hire juniors, a progressive policy answer.

steps.text: Practise checking and testing AI-written code on my side project
Take a 200-pound online cloud security course
Join the developers' union group and speak about junior hiring
Vote for a rule requiring firms to hire entry-level staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to stop pretending. In two years most of what I do is a machine's job, and everyone in tech knows it. At work I'd push Anselm to pivot the company toward things that need humans, and online I'd say we need a basic income pilot immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm terrified in a quiet way. Everything I trained for is thinking work. I'm 22, with a loan, no savings and no family money, and I'd have two years to figure out a life. Most people have no idea this is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save as hard as I can, probably 60 percent of my pay, and move into the cheapest room I can find. I'd look for hands-on or care work that I could live with, like a technician at the port, since the robots take three more years to get there. I'd also use the tools to build as many small products as I can, hoping one makes money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, then determined. Like waking up at 4 a.m. and then making a list. I like lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum, and what would you hold back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would I say to my mum? That I'm okay, and that I've got a plan, which would be a lie of about half. She works in a laundry, and she's proud that her daughter studied computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want a trade. How serious is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to learn something with my hands. I've never done anything with my hands except type, and that bothers me. Maybe an electrical apprenticeship, since the robots will need people who wire them.

say: I'd say we should **stop pretending**, since most of what I do becomes a machine's job in two years.
Online I'd call for a **basic income** pilot immediately.
think: I'm **terrified** in a quiet way, because everything I trained for is thinking work.
I'm 22 with a loan and **no savings**, with two years to build a life.
do: Save **60 percent** of my pay and move into the cheapest room I can find.
Look for **technician** work at the port, since robots arrive three years later.
Use the tools to build **small products**, hoping one makes money.
feel: I feel **scared**, then determined, like waking at 4 a.m. and making a list.
S2.quote: I'm 22, with a loan, no savings and no family money, and I'd have two years to figure out a life.
fieldNote: Elena's fear is **quiet and organised**: she moves straight to saving, side products and a physical trade.
She would soften the truth with her mother, who works in a laundry and is proud of her.
Mood is alarmed because her own field is the first reached and she has no cushion.

steps.text: Save 60 percent of my pay and move to the cheapest room
Apply for technician jobs at the port
Build and launch small paid tools using AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for people like me to adapt, but not for everyone. I'd say publicly that governments should start retraining schemes now and keep them open to workers of all ages. At work I'd suggest we use the time to build products that don't depend on cheap coding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit relieved, and a bit guilty about being relieved. By 2031 I'd be 27 with five years of experience in using these tools, which is more than most. But I'd worry about the people who haven't touched them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd specialise in something that's harder to automate, like safety-critical software or working with hardware. I'd pay off a big chunk of my loan by saving 40 percent of my pay and aim to have six months of living costs by 2029. I'd also help my flatmates with using AI at work, since I think a lot of people are being left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously optimistic. Like having a deadline that's far enough away to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would I do differently from the two-year scenario? I wouldn't panic-save, I'd invest in learning. I'd spend a little to take a degree in electronics at evenings, which wouldn't be the choice if I had two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the fear that stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one fear is that the next generation of juniors starts at a disadvantage. If the firms stop hiring juniors, who becomes the senior engineer in 2040? That's a real hole.

say: I'd say five years works for people like me but not **everyone**, so retraining must stay open to all ages.
At work I'd suggest products that don't rely on **cheap coding**.
think: I'd feel relieved and a bit **guilty**, because I'd have five years of experience with these tools.
I worry about people who haven't **touched** them.
do: Specialise in **safety-critical** software or hardware that's harder to automate.
Save **40 percent** of my pay and aim for six months' costs by 2029.
Help my **flatmates** use AI at work.
feel: I feel **cautiously optimistic**, like a deadline far enough away to plan around.
S3.quote: If the firms stop hiring juniors, who becomes the senior engineer in 2040? That's a real hole.
fieldNote: With five years Elena shifts from panic to **investing in learning**, such as evening electronics study.
She thinks about people who haven't used AI tools, which shows concern beyond herself.
She stays anxious because the entry-level pipeline itself is at risk.

steps.text: Start an evening electronics course aimed at hardware work
Save 40 percent of my pay toward six months of costs
Teach my flatmates to use AI tools at their jobs
Keep building my freight tool as a small paid product

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lot of time. I'd say we should treat it as the best chance we'll get to do things properly: free retraining, support for workers, rules about who owns the gains. It doesn't have to be a bad story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be fine, and that's an odd thing to say. By 2036 I'd be 32, with a decade of experience adapting. I might even run a small business that uses the new tools, since my side project could grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep moving up, but I'd also try to get into product work, where talking to people matters. I'd pay off the loan by 28, then save for a deposit. And I'd probably join a local committee to push for those retraining schemes, because I think I'd be good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. A bit excited, even. Ten years is a rare moment when you get to decide what the future looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you after ten years of notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The part I'd still worry about is inequality. If the gains go to the owners, ten years of preparing won't matter to people on the lowest pay. That's the part I'd work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hire a junior. Is that a promise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to use what I earn to hire another junior, if I ever run a company. I know that sounds a bit idealistic, but someone has to train the next lot.

say: I'd say ten years is the best chance to do things **properly**, with free retraining and rules on who owns the gains.
I'd add that it doesn't have to be a **bad** story.
think: I'd probably be **fine**, which feels odd to say.
At 32 I'd have a decade of experience **adapting** and maybe a small business.
do: Move into **product work**, where talking to people matters.
Pay off the loan by **28**, then save for a deposit.
Join a local **committee** pushing for retraining schemes.
feel: I feel **hopeful** and even excited about deciding what the future looks like.
S4.quote: Ten years is a rare moment when you get to decide what the future looks like.
fieldNote: Elena's reaction to ten years is **optimism**, joining a committee and caring about who gains.
She's the only person who frames the change as something to shape rather than survive.
Her remaining worry is inequality, not her own job.

steps.text: Move toward product work by talking to customers
Pay off the student loan by age 28
Join a local committee for worker retraining schemes
Grow my side project into a small company

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture, definitely. Not because I can't adapt, but because I'm adapting with no cushion and the people around me aren't ready. What would help is retraining that's free, a basic income to catch people, and firms required to hire entry-level staff.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I don't think I'm special for using the tools. I'm lucky to have been curious early, and a lot of people haven't had that luck. It should not be about luck.

headlineQuote: I don't think I'm special for using the tools. I'm lucky to have been curious early, and a lot of people haven't had that luck.
portrait: Elena is a **junior developer** at a freight-booking startup, renting a room and carrying heavy student debt with no family money.
She uses **AI tools** daily, hedges with side projects and trains for hardware-adjacent work.
Her politics are **progressive**: basic income, free retraining and rules forcing firms to hire juniors.
Her mood swings with the clock, from **alarm** at two years to calm at ten.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because she adapts well but has no cushion and her field is reached first.
whatWouldHelp: Free **retraining**, a basic income to catch people and a rule that firms hire entry-level staff.
